board.text: How many diameters from one point on a circle?

spec.note: One point on the circle

beats.say: Pick one point on a circle. How many diameters can be drawn from that point?

spec.note: A diameter goes straight through the centre

beats.say: First, what is a diameter? It is a straight line right across the circle that passes through the centre.

ask.ifNot: A line joining two points on the circle is a chord. It only earns the name diameter if it passes through the centre.

beats.say: From our point we can draw lots of straight lines across the circle. A line that misses the centre is called what?

board.text: misses the centre: just a chord

beats.say: So from our point there are plenty of chords. But a diameter has to aim straight at the centre.

spec.note: From one point, only 1 straight line passes through the centre

beats.say: And there is only one way to aim straight at the centre: go through it and carry on to the other side.
So from one point on the circle, only 1 diameter can be drawn.
The trap is the word many. A whole circle has endless diameters, but each one starts from a different point.

spec.note: As numbers: area = 3 × circumference

beats.say: For this circle, the area is 3 times the circumference, just as numbers. We have to find the radius.
We need the two rules. Area is pi times r times r. Circumference is 2 times pi times r.
3 lots of the circumference is 3 times 2 times pi times r. 3 times 2 is 6, so that is 6 times pi times r.
Now put the two side by side. Pi times r times r on the left. Pi times r times 6 on the right. Both have pi times r.

ask.ifNot: On the left, one r is still showing. On the right, the 6 is showing. For the sides to be equal, these two must be the same.

beats.say: Cover up the pi times r on both sides. What must the last r be, to make the two sides equal?
The r that is left must equal 6. So the radius is 6.
Check. With a radius of 6, r times r is 36. And 6 times r is 36 too. Both sides are 36 lots of pi.
No big sums were needed. When both sides share the same pieces, cover them up and compare what is left.

board.text: Circumference and area of a circle: same number

spec.note: Circumference and area are the same number

beats.say: The circumference and the area of a circle are the same number. We want the diameter.
Write the two rules. Circumference is 2 times pi times r. Area is pi times r times r.
They are equal. Pi times r times 2 on one side, pi times r times r on the other. Both sides have pi times r.

ask.ifNot: On the left, after covering pi times r, the 2 is left. On the right, one r is left.

beats.say: Cover up the pi times r on both sides. What is left on each side?
A 2 is left on one side and an r on the other. So r must be 2. The radius is 2 centimetres.
Careful! Is 2 our answer? Read the question again. It asks for the diameter, not the radius.
The diameter is twice the radius. 2 times 2 is 4.
The diameter is 4 centimetres.
Check: with radius 2, the circumference is 2 times 2 lots of pi, and the area is 2 times 2 lots of pi. Both are 4 lots of pi.

board.text: 8 circles in a rectangle: 2 rows of 4

spec.note: One circle fits in each square. Radius = 7 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Eight equal circles sit inside a rectangle in 2 rows of 4, touching each other and the sides. Each radius is 7 centimetres. What is the area of the rectangle?

ask.ifNot: 7 centimetres only reaches from the centre to the edge. From edge to edge is the diameter, which is two radii.

beats.say: The circles fill the rectangle from side to side. So how much room does one whole circle take up, from edge to edge?

spec.note: The diameter is twice the radius

beats.say: That's the trap: use the diameter, not the radius. 2 times 7 is 14 centimetres.

spec.note: The length holds 4 circles side by side

beats.say: 4 circles fit along the length. 4 times 14 is 56 centimetres.

spec.note: The breadth holds 2 circles

beats.say: 2 circles fit up the side. 2 times 14 is 28 centimetres.
Area is length times breadth: 56 times 28. Split 28 into 20 and 8.
56 times 20 is 1120. 56 times 8 is 448.
Add the parts: 1120 plus 448 makes 1568.
The area of the rectangle is 1568 square centimetres.
So: radius to diameter, count the circles each way to get the sides, then multiply.

spec.note: Circumference = 132 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: The circumference of a circle is 132 centimetres. We want its area.

ask.ifNot: The area rule is pi times radius times radius. So we need the radius, and the circumference can give it to us.

beats.say: We can't get the area straight from the circumference. What must we find first?
Circumference is 2 times 22 over 7 times r. 2 times 22 is 44. So it is 44 times r, divided by 7.
44 times something makes 132. Try it: 44 and 44 and 44 make 132. That is 3 lots.
So r divided by 7 is 3. That means r is 3 times 7, which is 21 centimetres.
Now the area: 22 over 7, times 21, times 21. Let the 7 divide first: 21 divided by 7 is 3.
That leaves 22 times 3 times 21. 22 times 3 is 66.
66 times 21: 66 times 20 is 1320, and one more 66 makes 1386.
The area is 1386 square centimetres.
Two stages: circumference gives the radius, then the radius gives the area. Don't rush the last multiplying.

board.text: Circumference = perimeter of rectangle 14 cm by 8 cm

spec.note: A circle's circumference equals this perimeter. Radius = ?

beats.say: A circle's circumference equals the perimeter of a rectangle, 14 centimetres by 8 centimetres. We want the circle's radius.
Start with the rectangle. 14 plus 8 is 22, and that is halfway round. Double it: 44 centimetres.
So the circle's circumference is 44 centimetres too. The rule is 2 times 22 over 7 times r.
2 times 22 is 44. So the circumference is 44 times r, divided by 7. And we know it equals 44.

ask.ifNot: 44 times something gives 44 again. Only multiplying by 1 leaves a number unchanged.

beats.say: 44 times r, divided by 7, gives back 44. So what must r divided by 7 be?
r divided by 7 is 1. So r is 7. The radius is 7 centimetres.
Check: 2 times 22 over 7 times 7. The 7s cancel, leaving 2 times 22, which is 44. It fits.
Careful with 14: that is the diameter of this circle, and also a side of the rectangle. The radius is 7.

board.text: Centre to any point on the circle: called the ?

spec.note: From the centre to a point on the circle

beats.say: What do we call the distance from the centre of a circle to any point on the circle?
Imagine drawing a circle with a compass. The needle sits at the centre, and the pencil goes round.

board.text: centre to circle: always the same

beats.say: The gap between the needle and the pencil never changes. So every point on the circle is the same distance from the centre.

ask.ifNot: The diameter goes all the way across. The circumference goes all the way round. From the centre out to the circle is the radius.

beats.say: That fixed distance has a name. Which one is it?
It is the radius: from the centre to the circle.
Think of the spokes of a cycle wheel. Each spoke runs from the centre to the rim, and each one is a radius.
So: centre to edge is the radius. Right across through the centre is the diameter.

board.text: The diameter of a circle is: ?

beats.say: How does the diameter of a circle compare with its radius?

board.text: diameter: right across, through the centre

beats.say: A radius goes from the centre out to the circle. A diameter goes right across the circle, through the centre.

ask.ifNot: From the edge to the centre is one radius. From the centre on to the other edge is one more.

beats.say: Walk along a diameter. You start on the circle, reach the centre, and carry on to the other side. How many radii did you walk?
One radius to the centre, and one more to the far side. 2 radii make a diameter.
So the diameter is twice the radius.
And the other way round: the radius is half the diameter. Don't mix up which one is bigger!
The diameter is always the longer one, because it goes all the way across.
The radius of a circle is 7 centimetres. What is its diameter?
The radius goes from the centre to the circle. The diameter goes right across, through the centre.

ask.ifNot: The diameter crosses the whole circle. The radius only gets as far as the centre. So the diameter is the longer one.

beats.say: So is the diameter bigger or smaller than the radius?
The diameter is two radii, end to end. 2 times 7 is 14.
The diameter is 14 centimetres.
Careful not to halve. Half of 7 would be smaller than the radius, and a diameter can never be shorter than a radius.
Check: 7 and 7 make 14.

board.text: The boundary of a circle is called the: ?

spec.note: The curved line that goes all the way round

beats.say: What is the boundary of a circle called?

board.text: boundary = the curved line all the way round

beats.say: The boundary is the edge: the curved line that goes all the way round the circle.
For a square or a rectangle, the distance round the edge is the perimeter. A circle has its own special word for it.

ask.ifNot: Area is the space inside. The diameter is a straight line across. The word for the curved line round the outside is circumference.

beats.say: Which word is it?
It is the circumference.
A way to remember: circumference starts like circle and circus. All of them are about going round.
So: radius and diameter are straight lines inside the circle. The circumference is the curved line around it.
A round plate has a diameter of 18 centimetres. What is its radius?
The diameter goes right across the plate, through the centre. The radius only goes from the centre to the edge.

ask.ifNot: The radius is the shorter one. It reaches only halfway across the plate. So we halve the diameter.

beats.say: So to get from the diameter to the radius, do we double or halve?
The radius is half the diameter. Half of 18 is 9.
The radius is 9 centimetres.
Check: 9 and 9 make 18, the full diameter.
Radius to diameter: double. Diameter to radius: halve. Ask yourself which one should be bigger.

board.text: Circle of diameter 12 cm, drawn with a compass.

spec.note: The compass opens from the centre to the circle

beats.say: Kiran wants to draw a circle of diameter 12 centimetres with a compass. How far apart should the needle and the pencil tip be?

board.text: needle: centre.  pencil: on the circle

beats.say: Think about how a compass works. The needle stays at the centre. The pencil travels round on the circle.

ask.ifNot: The gap runs from the centre to a point on the circle. Centre to circle is the radius.

beats.say: So the gap between the needle and the pencil is which part of the circle?
It is the radius. That's the trap: the question gives the diameter, but the compass is set to the radius.
The radius is half the diameter. Half of 12 is 6.
The needle and the pencil tip should be 6 centimetres apart.
If Kiran opened the compass to 12, the circle would come out twice as wide as he wanted.

spec.note: How long is the longest chord?

beats.say: A circle has a radius of 8 centimetres. How long is the longest chord that can be drawn in it?

board.text: Chord: joins two points on the circle

beats.say: A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circle. Short ones sit near the edge, longer ones nearer the middle.

ask.ifNot: A circle is widest across its middle. So the longest straight line inside it passes through the centre.

beats.say: Where does the very longest chord pass?
Through the centre. And a chord through the centre is the diameter.
The diameter is twice the radius. 2 times 8 is 16.
The longest chord is 16 centimetres.
The question never says the word diameter. You have to spot that the longest chord is the diameter.

board.text: Circle: radius 6 cm. P is 4 cm from the centre.

spec.note: P is 4 cm from the centre. Where is P?

beats.say: A circle has a radius of 6 centimetres. Point P is 4 centimetres from the centre. Where is P?

board.text: on the circle: exactly 6 cm away

beats.say: Every point on the circle is exactly 6 centimetres from the centre. That is what the radius tells us.

ask.ifNot: The circle is 6 centimetres away from the centre. You have only walked 4, so you are not there yet.

beats.say: Start at the centre and walk towards the circle. After 4 centimetres you stop. Have you reached the circle yet?
Not yet. 4 is less than 6.
So P is closer to the centre than the circle is. P is inside the circle.
Here is the rule. Less than the radius: inside. Equal to the radius: on the circle. More than the radius: outside.
So just compare the distance with the radius. Here 4 is less than 6, so P is inside.

board.text: O is the centre. A and B are on the circle.

spec.note: O is the centre. A and B are on the circle. OA = 7 cm

beats.say: O is the centre of a circle. A and B are two points on the circle. O A is 7 centimetres. How long is O B?

ask.ifNot: A line from the centre to the circle is a radius. A diameter would go right across, and a chord joins two points on the circle.

beats.say: O A joins the centre to a point on the circle. What do we call a line like that?

board.text: OA: a radius.  OB: a radius.

beats.say: O A is a radius. And O B also joins the centre to a point on the circle. So O B is a radius too.
Now the big fact about circles: every radius of the same circle has the same length.
So O B is the same as O A: 7 centimetres.
No sum was needed at all! It doesn't matter where B is on the circle. It is always one radius from the centre.

board.text: 4 circles in a row, each of radius 3 cm, touching.

spec.note: Four touching circles. First centre to last centre = ?

beats.say: Four equal circles, each of radius 3 centimetres, sit in a row, each touching the next. How far is it from the centre of the first to the centre of the last?

board.text: centre to next centre = radius + radius

beats.say: Start small. Take two circles that touch. From one centre you travel a radius to the touching point, then another radius to the next centre.
So neighbouring centres are 3 plus 3, which is 6 centimetres apart.

ask.ifNot: Hold up 4 fingers and count the spaces between them. There is always one gap fewer than the number of things.

beats.say: Now the tricky part. There are 4 centres in the row. How many gaps are there between the first and the last?
That's the trap: 4 circles, but only 3 gaps between their centres.
3 gaps of 6 centimetres. 3 times 6 is 18.
The distance from the first centre to the last is 18 centimetres.
The whole row is longer than that, because half a circle sticks out at each end. Centre to centre, count the gaps.

board.text: 6 bangles in a row, each of radius 4 cm, touching.

spec.note: Each bangle has radius 4 cm

beats.say: Six round bangles, each of radius 4 centimetres, lie in a straight row, each touching the next. How long is the row from end to end?

ask.ifNot: The radius only reaches from the centre to the edge. The full width of a bangle is its diameter, twice the radius.

beats.say: How much of the row does one bangle take up? Its full width, from one side to the other. Which measure is that?
The full width is the diameter. 2 times 4 is 8 centimetres.
The bangles touch, so there are no spaces between them. The row is just 6 bangles, side by side.
6 times 8 is 48.
The row is 48 centimetres long.
This time we want end to end, so every whole bangle counts. If it had asked centre to centre, we would count gaps instead.

board.text: Circle inside a square of side 10 cm, touching all sides.

spec.note: A circle inside just touches all four sides. Radius = ?

beats.say: A circle is drawn inside a square of side 10 centimetres, just touching all four sides. What is the radius of the circle?

ask.ifNot: The circle reaches from one side of the square to the opposite side. So it is exactly as wide as the square.

beats.say: The circle touches the left side and the right side of the square. So how wide is the circle, right across?
The circle is as wide as the square. So its diameter is 10 centimetres.
But the question asks for the radius, not the diameter.
The radius is half the diameter. Half of 10 is 5.
The radius of the circle is 5 centimetres.
A circle that fits snugly in a square has the square's side as its diameter. Then halve for the radius.

board.text: Circle of radius 6 cm fits exactly inside a square.

spec.note: A square fits round it, touching. Perimeter of the square = ?

beats.say: A circle of radius 6 centimetres fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the perimeter of the square?

ask.ifNot: The circle stretches right across the square, from one side to the other. Right across a circle is its diameter.

beats.say: The circle touches opposite sides of the square. So the side of the square is as long as which part of the circle?
The side of the square equals the diameter. 2 times 6 is 12 centimetres.
Careful: the side is 12, not 6. The radius only reaches halfway across the square.
A square has 4 equal sides. 4 times 12 is 48.
The perimeter of the square is 48 centimetres.
Two steps: radius to diameter gives the side, then 4 sides give the perimeter.

board.text: Two touching coins: radius 5 cm and radius 3 cm.

spec.note: Centre to centre, through the point where the coins touch

beats.say: Two coins lie flat and touch each other. One has a radius of 5 centimetres and the other 3 centimetres. How far apart are their centres?

ask.ifNot: Centre to edge is the radius. The big coin has a radius of 5 centimetres.

beats.say: Travel from one centre to the other. First you go from the centre of the big coin out to its edge. How far is that?

board.text: big coin: centre to edge = 5 cm

beats.say: 5 centimetres, one radius of the big coin. Now you are at the point where the coins touch.

board.text: small coin: edge to centre = 3 cm

beats.say: From there you go to the centre of the small coin. That is one radius of the small coin: 3 centimetres.
So the whole trip is 5 plus 3, which is 8.
The centres are 8 centimetres apart.
When two circles touch from outside, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius.

board.text: Same centre: radius 9 cm and radius 5 cm.

spec.note: Two circles with the same centre. Width of the ring = ?

beats.say: Two circles share the same centre. The big one has a radius of 9 centimetres and the small one 5 centimetres. How wide is the ring between them?

board.text: small circle at 5 cm, big circle at 9 cm

beats.say: Walk out from the centre in a straight line. After 5 centimetres you cross the small circle. After 9 centimetres you reach the big circle.

ask.ifNot: The ring is the gap between the 5 centimetre mark and the 9 centimetre mark. To find a gap, we subtract.

beats.say: The ring is the stretch between the two circles. How do we find its width?
9 minus 5 is 4.
The ring is 4 centimetres wide.
Check: 5 centimetres to the small circle, then 4 more across the ring, brings you to 9.
For circles with the same centre, the gap between them is the difference of the radii.
The diameter of a circle is 12 centimetres longer than its radius. What is the radius?
We always know one thing about a diameter. It is made of two radii, end to end.
And the question tells us the diameter is the radius plus 12 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Line one says radius plus radius. Line two says radius plus 12. The second part of each must match.

beats.say: Look at the two lines together. Both start with one radius. So what must the 12 centimetres be?
The extra 12 is the second radius! So the radius is 12 centimetres.
Check: the diameter is 12 plus 12, which is 24. And 24 is 12 more than 12. It fits.
The trap is to halve 12 and say 6. Don't halve just because you see the word diameter. Read what the 12 really is.

board.text: NOT a chord length: 4, 9, 12 or 13 cm?

spec.note: Which length cannot be a chord?

beats.say: A circle has a radius of 6 centimetres. Which of these cannot be the length of a chord: 4, 9, 12 or 13 centimetres?

board.text: Chord: joins two points on the circle

beats.say: A chord joins two points on the circle. Chords can be tiny, near the edge. But there is a limit to how long one can be.

ask.ifNot: A radius starts at the centre, so it is not a chord. The longest chord goes right across through the centre: the diameter.

beats.say: Which chord is the longest one of all?
The diameter. For this circle that is 2 times 6, which is 12 centimetres.
So a chord can be any length up to 12, but never more. 4 fits. 9 fits. 12 is the diameter itself, so it fits too.
But 13 is more than 12. No chord can be longer than the diameter.
So 13 centimetres cannot be a chord of this circle.
Careful with 12: it looks too big next to a radius of 6, but it is exactly the diameter. Compare with the diameter, not the radius.

board.text: Tray 20 cm by 8 cm. Biscuits of radius 2 cm, in rows.

spec.note: Round biscuits of radius 2 cm, in straight rows

beats.say: A tray is 20 centimetres long and 8 centimetres wide. Round biscuits of radius 2 centimetres are laid on it in straight rows. What is the most that can fit?

ask.ifNot: 2 centimetres is only the radius, from the centre to the edge. The full width is the diameter, twice that.

beats.say: How much room does one biscuit need? Its full width, in every direction. What is the full width of a biscuit?
Here's the trap: a biscuit takes up its diameter, not its radius. 2 times 2 is 4 centimetres.
Along the 20 centimetre length: 20 divided by 4 is 5. So 5 biscuits fit in a row.
Across the 8 centimetre width: 8 divided by 4 is 2. So there is room for 2 rows.
2 rows of 5 biscuits. 5 times 2 is 10.
The tray holds 10 biscuits.
So: find the full width of one circle, see how many fit each way, then multiply.

board.text: Wire: circle of radius 7 cm, then a square.

spec.note: The same wire is bent into a square. Side = ?

beats.say: A wire is bent into a circle of radius 7 centimetres. Then the same wire is bent into a square. What is the side of the square? Use 22 over 7 for pi.

ask.ifNot: The wire is the curved edge of the circle. The distance round a circle is its circumference.

beats.say: The wire goes once round the circle. So the length of the wire is the circle's what?
The circumference is 2 times pi times the radius.
The 7 underneath and the radius 7 cancel each other. That leaves 2 times 22, which is 44.
So the wire is 44 centimetres long. Now it becomes a square with 4 equal sides.
44 divided by 4 is 11.
The side of the square is 11 centimetres.
Same wire, same length. The circumference of the circle becomes the perimeter of the square.

board.text: Big radius = small diameter. Small radius = 3 cm.

spec.note: Its diameter is the radius of a big circle

beats.say: The radius of a big circle equals the diameter of a small circle. The small circle's radius is 3 centimetres. What is the big circle's diameter?
Lots of radius and diameter words here! Go one step at a time. Start with the small circle. Its diameter is twice its radius.

ask.ifNot: Read the first sentence again: the radius of the big circle equals the diameter of the small circle.

beats.say: The small diameter is 6 centimetres. The question says that this is the same as the big circle's what?
It is the big circle's radius. So the big radius is 6 centimetres.
Careful: don't stop at 6! We want the big circle's diameter, which is twice its radius.
2 times 6 is 12.
The diameter of the big circle is 12 centimetres.
We doubled twice: 3 to 6, then 6 to 12. Label each number as you go, so you always know what it is.

board.text: 3 circles, radius 4 cm, each touching the other two.

spec.note: A, B, C: centres of touching circles of radius 4 cm

beats.say: Three equal circles with centres A, B and C each have a radius of 4 centimetres. Each touches the other two. What is the perimeter of triangle A B C?
Look at one side of the triangle, from A to B. It starts at one centre and ends at the other, passing through the point where the circles touch.

ask.ifNot: From A to the touching point is one radius, 4 centimetres. From there to B is another radius.

beats.say: So how long is the side A B?
One radius and then another: 4 plus 4 is 8 centimetres.
The circles are all the same size, so the other two sides are 8 centimetres as well.
The triangle has 3 sides of 8. 3 times 8 is 24.
The perimeter of triangle A B C is 24 centimetres.
Whenever circles touch, the line between their centres is one radius plus the other radius.

board.text: 10 circles in a rectangle: 2 rows of 5.
Perimeter = 84 cm. Radius of each circle = ?

spec.note: One circle in each square. Perimeter = 84 cm. Radius = ?

beats.say: Ten equal circles sit inside a rectangle in 2 rows of 5, touching each other and the sides. The rectangle's perimeter is 84 centimetres. What is each circle's radius?
Let's measure the rectangle in diameters. The length holds 5 circles, so it is 5 diameters. The width holds 2 circles, so it is 2 diameters.
So length plus width is 5 plus 2, which is 7 diameters.

choices: No, 7 diameters is only half of it
ask.ifNot: The perimeter is two lengths and two widths. One length plus one width is only halfway round.

beats.say: Now, the perimeter is 84. Is 84 equal to those 7 diameters?
That's the trap. Length plus width is half the perimeter. Half of 84 is 42.
So 7 diameters make 42. 42 divided by 7 is 6. Each diameter is 6 centimetres.
One last step: the question asks for the radius. Half of 6 is 3.
The radius of each circle is 3 centimetres.
Check: the length is 5 times 6, which is 30. The width is 2 times 6, which is 12. 30 plus 12 is 42, and double is 84.

board.text: Small circle (radius 3 cm) inside big circle (radius 10 cm).
They touch at one point. Centres are ? apart

spec.note: Both end at the point where the circles touch

beats.say: A small circle of radius 3 centimetres lies inside a big circle of radius 10 centimetres, touching it at one point. How far apart are the two centres?

board.text: touching point, small centre, big centre: one line

beats.say: Stand at the touching point and look inwards. Both centres are straight ahead of you, on one line.

board.text: big centre: 10 cm in.  small centre: 3 cm in.

beats.say: The big centre is 10 centimetres from the touching point. The small centre is 3 centimetres from it. Both in the same direction.

ask.ifNot: Both centres are on the same side of the touching point. One is 3 in and the other is 10 in. The gap between them is the difference.

beats.say: So how far is it from one centre to the other?
10 minus 3 is 7.
The centres are 7 centimetres apart.
Here's the trap. When circles touch from outside, we add the radii. When one is inside the other, we subtract.

board.text: Circles of radius 2 cm, 3 cm, 4 cm in a row, touching.

spec.note: Three touching circles in a row. First centre to last = ?

beats.say: Three circles of radius 2, 3 and 4 centimetres are in a row, centres on one line. The middle one touches the other two. How far is it from the first centre to the last centre?
Let's take the trip in three parts. Part one: from the first centre out to its edge. That is its radius, 2 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: We go in one side of the middle circle and out the other. That is its full width, the diameter, which is twice 3.

beats.say: Part two: we must cross the whole middle circle, from one side to the other. How far is that?
That's the trap: the middle circle is crossed completely, so we need its diameter. 2 times 3 is 6.
Part three: from the edge of the last circle in to its centre. That is its radius, 4 centimetres. We stop at the centre.
Add the three parts. 2 plus 6 plus 4 is 12.
The distance between the first and last centres is 12 centimetres.
Centre to centre: one radius for each end circle, but a whole diameter for any circle in between.

board.text: Circle: circumference 88 cm, fits exactly in a square.

spec.note: Circumference = 88 cm. The circle fits exactly inside a square

beats.say: A circle has a circumference of 88 centimetres. It fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the side of the square? Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The circle touches opposite sides of the square. So the side of the square equals the circle's diameter. We need the radius first.
Circumference is 2 times 22 over 7 times r. 2 times 22 is 44. So it is 44 times r, divided by 7.
44 times something makes 88. That something is 2.
So r divided by 7 is 2. That means r is 2 times 7, which is 14 centimetres.

choices: No, the side is the diameter
ask.ifNot: The radius only reaches from the centre to one side of the square. The circle stretches right across, so the side is the diameter.

beats.say: The radius is 14. Is that the side of the square?
The side is the diameter: 2 times 14 is 28.
The side of the square is 28 centimetres.
Another trap is sharing 88 among 4 sides. The 88 goes round the circle, not round the square.

board.text: Square sheet of side 14 cm. Circle of radius 7 cm cut out.

spec.note: A circle of radius 7 cm is cut out of this sheet

beats.say: A circle of radius 7 centimetres is cut out of a square sheet of side 14 centimetres. What area of paper is left? Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The paper left is the square with the circle taken away. So we need two areas.
The square: 14 times 14. 14 times 10 is 140, and 14 times 4 is 56. Together, 196.

ask.ifNot: 2 times pi times the radius is the distance round, the circumference. For the space inside, the radius is used twice.

beats.say: Now the circle. Which rule gives the area of a circle?
Pi times radius times radius: 22 over 7, times 7, times 7. One 7 cancels the 7 underneath, leaving 22 times 7.
22 times 7 is 154.
Take the circle from the square. 196 minus 154 is 42.
The area of paper left is 42 square centimetres.
Careful to take away the circle's area, not its circumference. Area from area, always.

board.text: 5 points on a circle. Every pair is joined.

beats.say: Five points are marked on a circle. Every pair of points is joined by a straight line. How many chords are drawn?
Let's count in order so we don't count any chord twice. Call the points 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.
From point 1, chords go to each of the other 4 points. That is 4 chords.

ask.ifNot: Point 2 can join points 3, 4 and 5. Its chord to point 1 is already drawn, so we don't count it again.

beats.say: Now point 2. It is already joined to point 1. So how many new chords start from point 2?
3 new chords. Then point 3 gives 2 new ones, and point 4 gives just 1. Point 5 is already joined to everyone.
Add them up: 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 is 10.
10 chords are drawn.
The trap is 5 times 4, which is 20. That counts every chord twice, once from each end. And half of 20 is 10.

board.text: Two trays of side 24 cm: 3 rows of 3, and 4 rows of 4.

spec.note: First tray: 3 rows of 3. Second tray: 4 rows of 4

beats.say: Two square trays each have a side of 24 centimetres. One is filled by 9 plates in 3 rows of 3. The other by 16 plates in 4 rows of 4. How much longer is a plate's radius in the first tray?
First tray: 3 plates fit across 24 centimetres. So each plate is 24 divided by 3, which is 8 centimetres wide.

ask.ifNot: The full width of a round plate, from one side to the other, is its diameter. The radius is half of that.

beats.say: 8 centimetres is the full width of a plate. Is that its radius or its diameter?
It is the diameter. So the radius is half of 8, which is 4 centimetres.
Second tray: 4 plates across. 24 divided by 4 is 6 centimetres wide, so the radius is half of 6, which is 3.
Now compare the radii. 4 minus 3 is 1.
The radius in the first tray is 1 centimetre longer.
The trap is comparing the diameters, 8 and 6. The question asks about the radii, so halve first, then subtract.

board.text: Wire 132 cm, cut into 3 equal pieces. Each makes a circle.

spec.note: Each piece is bent into a circle. Radius = ?

beats.say: A wire 132 centimetres long is cut into 3 equal pieces. Each piece is bent into a circle. What is the radius of each circle? Use 22 over 7 for pi.
Careful: the whole wire does not make one circle. First cut it. 132 divided by 3 is 44 centimetres for each piece.

ask.ifNot: The wire is bent to make the edge of the circle. The distance all the way round the edge is the circumference.

beats.say: One piece goes once round its circle. So 44 centimetres is that circle's what?
It is the circumference. And circumference is 2 times 22 over 7 times r. 2 times 22 is 44, so that is 44 times r, divided by 7.
44 times r, divided by 7, must give 44. So r divided by 7 is 1, and r is 7.
The radius of each circle is 7 centimetres.
Check: 2 times 22 over 7 times 7. The 7s cancel, and 2 times 22 is 44. That is one piece of wire.
So: cut first, then treat each piece as a circumference and work back to the radius.

board.text: 12 circles in a rectangle: 3 rows of 4.
Area of rectangle = 432 sq cm. Radius = ?

spec.note: One circle in each square. Area = 432 sq cm. Radius = ?

beats.say: Twelve equal circles sit inside a rectangle in 3 rows of 4, touching each other and the sides. The rectangle's area is 432 square centimetres. What is each circle's radius?

board.text: 12 equal little squares fill the rectangle

beats.say: Imagine a little square box drawn round every circle. The 12 boxes fill the rectangle exactly, like tiles.
So the 432 is shared equally among 12 little squares. 432 divided by 12 is 36. Check: 12 times 30 is 360, 12 times 6 is 72, and together they make 432.

ask.ifNot: Area of a square is side times side. Which number times itself makes 36? Try 6 times 6.

beats.say: A little square has an area of 36. How long is its side?
6 times 6 is 36. So each little square has a side of 6 centimetres.

board.text: side of little square = diameter = 6 cm

beats.say: The circle just fits its square. So the side of the square, 6, is the circle's diameter. Don't stop here!
The question asks for the radius. Half of 6 is 3.
The radius of each circle is 3 centimetres.
Check: the rectangle is 4 times 6 long, which is 24, and 3 times 6 wide, which is 18. And 24 times 18 is 432.

board.text: Pond: radius 7 m. Path 7 m wide all round.

spec.note: A path 7 m wide runs all the way round this pond

beats.say: A round pond has a radius of 7 metres. A path 7 metres wide runs all the way round it. What is the area of the path? Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The path is a ring. A ring is a big circle with a smaller circle taken out of its middle.

ask.ifNot: From the centre, go 7 metres to the edge of the pond. Then 7 more metres across the path.

beats.say: The big circle is the pond and the path together. What is its radius?
7 for the pond and 7 more for the path: 14 metres.
Big circle: 22 over 7, times 14, times 14. 14 divided by 7 is 2. So we have 22 times 2 times 14.
22 times 2 is 44. 44 times 14: 44 times 10 is 440, and 44 times 4 is 176. Together, 616.
The pond: 22 over 7, times 7, times 7. One 7 cancels. That leaves 22 times 7, which is 154.
Take the pond out of the big circle. 616 minus 154 is 462.
The area of the path is 462 square metres.
Surprised? The path is as wide as the pond's radius, but its area is 3 times the pond's. Rings on the outside are big!

board.text: Radius doubled: circumference grows by 88 cm.

spec.note: The radius is made twice as long

beats.say: When a circle's radius is made twice as long, its circumference becomes 88 centimetres longer. What was the radius at the start? Use 22 over 7 for pi.

ask.ifNot: The radius is multiplied into the circumference. Make the radius twice as big, and the whole answer is twice as big.

beats.say: Circumference is 2 times pi times the radius. If we double the radius, what happens to the circumference?
It doubles. So the new circumference is the old one, and then the old one again.
Here's the key. The extra part is exactly one old circumference. And the extra part is 88. So the old circumference was 88.
Careful: 88 is not the new circumference. It is the amount it grew, which equals the old one.
Now find the radius. 2 times 22 is 44, so the circumference is 44 times r, divided by 7. 88 divided by 44 is 2.
So r divided by 7 is 2, and r is 2 times 7, which is 14.
The radius at the start was 14 centimetres.
Check: the doubled radius is 28. Its circumference is 44 times 4, which is 176. And 176 minus 88 is 88. It grew by 88.

board.text: 7 points on a circle. Join each to all but its 2 neighbours.

beats.say: Seven points are marked on a circle. Each point is joined to every other point, except the two right next to it. How many chords are drawn?
Stand on one point. There are 7 points in all. You can't join to yourself, and you skip your 2 neighbours. That rules out 3 points.

ask.ifNot: 7 points, and 3 of them are ruled out: yourself and your two neighbours. Take 3 from 7.

beats.say: So how many chords leave your point?
7 minus 3 is 4. Each point sends out 4 chords.
7 points with 4 chords each: 7 times 4 is 28. But wait. Is 28 the answer?
Here's the trap. Every chord has two ends, so we counted each chord twice: once from each end.
So we halve it. Half of 28 is 14.
14 chords are drawn.
Counting from every point is quick, but remember that each line gets counted from both of its ends. Halve at the end.

board.text: 8 equally spaced points on a circle. Every pair is joined.
How many chords are NOT diameters?

beats.say: Eight points are equally spaced round a circle. Every pair is joined by a chord. How many of these chords are not diameters?
Plan: count all the chords, then take away the ones that are diameters.
All the chords. The first point joins 7 others. The next gives 6 new chords, then 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1.

ask.ifNot: A diameter passes through the centre. That happens only when the two points are straight across the circle from each other.

beats.say: That adds up to 28 chords. Now, when is a chord a diameter?
A diameter joins two opposite points. 8 points make 4 opposite pairs. So there are 4 diameters.
Careful: not 8 diameters. Each diameter uses up 2 points, one at each end.
Take the diameters away. 28 minus 4 is 24.
24 of the chords are not diameters.
When a question says not, count everything first, then take away the ones you don't want.

board.text: Small circle inside big circle: touches it at one point
and passes through its centre. Big diameter = 24 cm.

spec.note: A small circle inside touches it and passes through its centre

beats.say: A small circle inside a big circle touches it at one point, and also passes through the big circle's centre. The big diameter is 24 centimetres. How far apart are the centres?
Start with the big circle. Its radius is half of 24, which is 12 centimetres.

board.text: touching point to big centre = 12 cm

beats.say: So from the touching point to the big centre is 12 centimetres. The small circle passes through both of those points.

ask.ifNot: The two points are on opposite sides of the small circle, as far apart as they can be. That full width is its diameter.

beats.say: The small circle stretches from the touching point right across to the big centre. So that 12 centimetres is the small circle's what?
It is the small circle's diameter. And the small centre sits halfway along a diameter.
Half of 12 is 6. So the small centre is 6 centimetres from the big centre.
The centres are 6 centimetres apart.
We halved twice: 24 to 12 for the big radius, then 12 to 6 for the small radius. Each halving had its own reason.

board.text: 3 touching coins. Centres are 7 cm, 8 cm, 9 cm apart.

spec.note: The corners are the centres of the three coins

beats.say: Three coins of different sizes each touch the other two. The distances between their centres are 7, 8 and 9 centimetres. What is the radius of the largest coin?
When two coins touch, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius. So each distance is two radii added.

ask.ifNot: Each coin touches two others. So its radius is part of two of the distances.

beats.say: Add all three distances: 7 plus 8 plus 9 is 24. In that total, how many times is each coin's radius counted?
Twice! So 24 is every radius counted twice. Halve it: the three radii add up to 12.
The two smaller coins have the closest centres: 7 centimetres. So their two radii add up to 7.
All three radii make 12. The two smaller ones make 7. So the largest is 12 minus 7, which is 5.
The radius of the largest coin is 5 centimetres.
Check: the radii are 3, 4 and 5. 3 plus 4 is 7. 3 plus 5 is 8. 4 plus 5 is 9. All three distances match!
The trap is halving the 9. That only works for two equal coins, and these are all different.

board.text: 2 touching tins, radius 7 cm. A tight ribbon round both.

beats.say: Two round tins of radius 7 centimetres stand touching. A ribbon is pulled tight round both: straight across on two sides, and curving round the outer half of each tin. How long is it?
Split the ribbon into easy pieces: two straight parts, and two curved parts.
A straight part runs from one tin across to the other. It is as long as the gap between the centres: one radius plus one radius.
There is a straight part on both sides. 2 times 14 is 28.

ask.ifNot: Half and half make one whole. The two curved parts together are the same as going once round one tin.

beats.say: Now the curves. The ribbon goes round half of one tin and half of the other. What do two half circles make?
One whole circle! Its circumference is 2 times 22 over 7 times 7. The 7s cancel, leaving 2 times 22, which is 44.
Add the straight parts and the curved parts. 28 plus 44 is 72.
The ribbon is 72 centimetres long.
The trap is going right round both tins: 2 times 44, which is 88. The ribbon only hugs the outer half of each tin.

board.text: Hour hand 7 cm long. One day = 24 hours.

spec.note: The tip of the hour hand moves round this circle

beats.say: The hour hand of a clock is 7 centimetres long. How far does its tip travel in one full day of 24 hours? Use 22 over 7 for pi.

board.text: tip moves on a circle of radius 7 cm

beats.say: As the hand turns, its tip draws a circle. The hand is the radius of that circle: 7 centimetres.
Once round is the circumference: 2 times 22 over 7 times 7. The 7s cancel, leaving 2 times 22, which is 44.

ask.ifNot: The minute hand goes round in 1 hour. The hour hand is slow: it creeps from 12 all the way back to 12 in 12 hours.

beats.say: Now think about the clock. How long does the hour hand take to go once round?
12 hours for one round. A day has 24 hours, so the hour hand goes round 24 divided by 12 times: that is 2 rounds.
2 rounds of 44 centimetres. 2 times 44 is 88.
The tip of the hour hand travels 88 centimetres in a day.
Two traps: stopping at one round, or thinking the hour hand goes round every hour. That one is the minute hand!

board.text: 8 circles in a rectangle: 2 rows of 4

spec.note: One circle fits in each square. Radius = 6 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Eight equal circles sit in a rectangle in 2 rows of 4, touching each other and the sides. Each radius is 6 centimetres. Find the perimeter of the rectangle.

ask.ifNot: 6 centimetres only reaches from the centre to the edge. From edge to edge is the diameter, two radii.

beats.say: The circles fill the rectangle from side to side. How much room does one circle take, from edge to edge?

spec.note: Diameter = 2 × 6

beats.say: That's the first trap: use the diameter, not the radius. 2 times 6 is 12 centimetres.

spec.note: The length holds 4 circles, the breadth holds 2

beats.say: The length holds 4 circles: 4 times 12 is 48. The breadth holds 2 circles: 2 times 12 is 24.

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth cover only two of the four sides. The other two sides are still to come.

beats.say: Now the perimeter. Length plus breadth is 48 plus 24, which is 72. Are we finished?
72 is only halfway round. That's the second trap! Double it: 2 times 72 is 144.
The perimeter of the rectangle is 144 centimetres.
Two things to remember: a circle takes up its diameter, and a perimeter goes round all four sides.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Here is a circle with a radius of 21 centimetres. We want its area, using 22 over 7 for pi.
The area is the space inside the circle. The rule is pi times the radius times the radius.

ask.ifNot: The 2 belongs to the circumference, the distance round. For the space inside, the radius is used twice: pi times 21 times 21.

beats.say: Which sum is that for our circle?
Careful: the radius goes in twice, and there is no 2 in this rule. Now let the 7 divide first. 21 divided by 7 is 3.
So we have 22 times 3 times 21. 22 times 3 is 66.
Now 66 times 21. Split 21 into 20 and 1.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 66 times 20 is 1320. 66 times 1 is 66. What do the two parts make together?
1320 plus 66 makes 1386.
There it is: the area is 1386 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because it is an area.
Does that look sensible? 21 times 21 is 441. A circle's area is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 441 is 1323, so 1386 fits.
Remember: area is pi times radius times radius. The rule with the 2 in it is for the circumference.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Here is a circle with a radius of 35 centimetres. We want its circumference, using 22 over 7 for pi.
Circumference means the distance right round the edge of the circle. Think of an ant walking once round the rim.

ask.ifNot: For going round the circle we need the 2 as well. Circumference is 2 times pi times the radius, and the radius goes in just once.

beats.say: The rule is 2 times pi times the radius. Which sum is that for our circle?
Here's a trick to keep the numbers small. Divide the 35 by the 7 first. 35 divided by 7 is 5.
Now it is just 2 times 22 times 5. First, 2 times 22 is 44.
Then 44 times 5 is 220.
So the circumference is 220 centimetres.
Does that look sensible? The circle is 70 centimetres across. Going round is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 70 is 210, so 220 fits.
So for a circumference: 2 times pi times the radius. And divide by the 7 first to keep the sum small.

board.text: All points equidistant from a fixed point called the: ?

spec.note: Every point on the circle is this far from one fixed point

beats.say: A circle is all the points that are the same distance from one fixed point. What is that fixed point called?
Equidistant is a long word. It just means the same distance away.

ask.ifNot: The rope keeps the goat the same distance from the post all the time. That makes a perfectly round path.

beats.say: Think of a goat tied to a post by a rope. It walks round as far out as the rope lets it. What shape is its path?
A circle! The goat is always the same distance from the post. So the post is the fixed point, right in the middle.
That middle point of a circle is called the centre.
And the rope? Its length is the radius. Careful: the radius is a distance, but the question asks for a point.
So: the centre is the point in the middle. The radius is how far the circle is from it.
The radius of a circle is 9.5 centimetres. What is its diameter?
The diameter goes right across the circle through the centre. That is one radius, then another radius.

ask.ifNot: The diameter is the longer one. It is made of two radii, so we need 2 lots of 9.5.

beats.say: So what do we do to 9.5?
Double it. 2 times 9 is 18. And 2 times 0.5 is two halves, which make 1.
18 plus 1 is 19.
The diameter is 19 centimetres.
Don't let the decimal worry you. Double the whole part, double the half, and put them together.

board.text: The longest chord of a circle is called the: ?

beats.say: What is the longest chord of a circle called?

board.text: Chord: straight line, two points on the circle

beats.say: A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circle.

ask.ifNot: A circle is widest right across its middle. So the longest chord is the one that passes through the centre.

beats.say: A chord near the edge is short. As it slides towards the middle it grows. Where is it longest?

spec.note: A chord is longest when it passes through the centre

beats.say: Through the centre. No chord can be longer than that one.
A chord through the centre is called the diameter.
Watch the other names. An arc is curved, and the circumference goes round. A radius stops at the centre, so it is not a chord.
So the diameter is a chord, and it is the longest one a circle can have.

board.text: How many axes of symmetry does a circle have?

beats.say: How many axes of symmetry does a circle have?

board.text: Axis of symmetry = a fold line that matches

beats.say: An axis of symmetry is a fold line. Fold along it, and the two halves match exactly.

board.text: top to bottom: yes.  side to side: yes.

beats.say: Take a paper circle. Fold it top to bottom, through the centre. The halves match. Now fold it side to side. They match again.

ask.ifNot: A circle is equally round everywhere. However you turn it, a fold through the centre gives two equal halves.

beats.say: Now tilt the fold a little, still through the centre. Do the halves still match?

spec.note: Every diameter cuts the circle into two matching halves

beats.say: They do! Any fold through the centre works. Every diameter is an axis of symmetry.
And how many diameters are there? You can keep tilting the line a tiny bit more, for ever. There is no end to them.
So a circle has an infinite number of axes of symmetry. Infinite means without end.
A square has 4 and a rectangle has 2. The circle beats them all, because it is the same in every direction.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Find the circumference of a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The circumference is the distance round the circle. It is pi times the diameter.

ask.ifNot: The diameter is two radii, end to end. So we double 21.

beats.say: We are given the radius, 21. So what is the diameter?
Double 21 is 42. Careful not to skip this step: pi times the radius alone gives only half of the way round.
Now 22 over 7, times 42. Let the 7 divide first: 42 divided by 7 is 6.
That leaves 22 times 6. 20 times 6 is 120, and 2 times 6 is 12. Together, 132.
The circumference is 132 centimetres.
Does it look sensible? Going round is a bit more than 3 times the diameter. 3 times 42 is 126, so 132 fits.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Here is a circle with a radius of 28 centimetres. We want its area, using 22 over 7 for pi.
The area is the space inside the circle. The rule is pi times the radius times the radius.

ask.ifNot: The 2 belongs to the circumference, the distance round. For the space inside, the radius is used twice: pi times 28 times 28.

beats.say: Which sum is that for our circle?
Careful: the radius goes in twice, and there is no 2 in this rule. Now let the 7 divide first. 28 divided by 7 is 4.
So we have 22 times 4 times 28. 22 times 4 is 88.
Now 88 times 28. Split 28 into 20 and 8.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 88 times 20 is 1760. 88 times 8 is 704. What do the two parts make together?
1760 plus 704 makes 2464.
There it is: the area is 2464 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because it is an area.
Does that look sensible? 28 times 28 is 784. A circle's area is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 784 is 2352, so 2464 fits.
So for the area of a circle: pi times radius times radius. No 2 in it, and the answer is in square units.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Here is a circle with a radius of 14 centimetres. We want its circumference, using 22 over 7 for pi.
The circumference is the distance all the way round the circle. It is like a perimeter, but for a round shape.

ask.ifNot: For going round the circle we need the 2 as well. Circumference is 2 times pi times the radius, and the radius goes in just once.

beats.say: The rule is 2 times pi times the radius. Which sum is that for our circle?
Before we multiply, let's make it easy. The 7 underneath divides into 14. 14 divided by 7 is 2.
Now it is just 2 times 22 times 2. First, 2 times 22 is 44.
Then 44 times 2 is 88.
So the circumference is 88 centimetres.
Does that look sensible? The circle is 28 centimetres across. Going round is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 28 is 84, so 88 fits.
Remember the plan: 2 times pi times the radius. Don't leave out the 2, and let the 7 divide first.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Here is a circle with a radius of 28 centimetres. We want its circumference, using 22 over 7 for pi.
Circumference means the distance right round the edge of the circle. Think of an ant walking once round the rim.

ask.ifNot: For going round the circle we need the 2 as well. Circumference is 2 times pi times the radius, and the radius goes in just once.

beats.say: The rule is 2 times pi times the radius. Which sum is that for our circle?
Here's a trick to keep the numbers small. Divide the 28 by the 7 first. 28 divided by 7 is 4.
Now it is just 2 times 22 times 4. First, 2 times 22 is 44.
Then 44 times 4 is 176.
So the circumference is 176 centimetres.
Does that look sensible? The circle is 56 centimetres across. Going round is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 56 is 168, so 176 fits.
So for a circumference: 2 times pi times the radius. And divide by the 7 first to keep the sum small.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: This circle has a radius of 7 centimetres. Our job is to find its circumference. For pi we use 22 over 7.
Circumference means the distance right round the edge of the circle. Think of an ant walking once round the rim.

ask.ifNot: For going round the circle we need the 2 as well. Circumference is 2 times pi times the radius, and the radius goes in just once.

beats.say: The rule is 2 times pi times the radius. Which sum is that for our circle?
Here's a trick to keep the numbers small. The 7 underneath and the radius 7 cancel each other. 7 divided by 7 is 1.
Now it is just 2 times 22 times 1. 2 times 22 is 44, and 44 times 1 is still 44.
So the circumference is 44 centimetres.
Does that look sensible? The circle is 14 centimetres across. Going round is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 14 is 42, so 44 fits.
So for a circumference: 2 times pi times the radius. And divide by the 7 first to keep the sum small.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Find the circumference of a circle with diameter 14 centimetres. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The circumference is pi times the diameter.

ask.ifNot: Read the question once more. It says diameter 14 centimetres. So there is no need to double it.

beats.say: Look carefully at what we are given. Is 14 the radius or the diameter?
It is already the diameter. That's the trap: don't double it again! We just need 22 over 7, times 14.
Let the 7 divide first. 14 divided by 7 is 2.
That leaves 22 times 2, which is 44.
The circumference is 44 centimetres.
Sensible? A bit more than 3 times the diameter. 3 times 14 is 42, so 44 fits.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: This circle has a radius of 35 centimetres. Our job is to find its area. For pi we use 22 over 7.
The area is the space inside the circle. The rule is pi times the radius times the radius.

ask.ifNot: The 2 belongs to the circumference, the distance round. For the space inside, the radius is used twice: pi times 35 times 35.

beats.say: Which sum is that for our circle?
Careful: the radius goes in twice, and there is no 2 in this rule. Now let the 7 divide first. 35 divided by 7 is 5.
So we have 22 times 5 times 35. 22 times 5 is 110.
Now 110 times 35. Split 35 into 30 and 5.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 110 times 30 is 3300. 110 times 5 is 550. What do the two parts make together?
3300 plus 550 makes 3850.
So the area is 3850 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area measures the space inside.
Does that look sensible? 35 times 35 is 1225. A circle's area is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 1225 is 3675, so 3850 fits.
So for the area of a circle: pi times radius times radius. No 2 in it, and the answer is in square units.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Here is a circle with a radius of 14 centimetres. We want its area, using 22 over 7 for pi.
The area is the space inside the circle. The rule is pi times the radius times the radius.

ask.ifNot: The 2 belongs to the circumference, the distance round. For the space inside, the radius is used twice: pi times 14 times 14.

beats.say: Which sum is that for our circle?
Careful: the radius goes in twice, and there is no 2 in this rule. Now let the 7 divide first. 14 divided by 7 is 2.
So we have 22 times 2 times 14. 22 times 2 is 44.
Now 44 times 14. Split 14 into 10 and 4.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 44 times 10 is 440. 44 times 4 is 176. What do the two parts make together?
440 plus 176 makes 616.
There it is: the area is 616 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because it is an area.
Does that look sensible? 14 times 14 is 196. A circle's area is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 196 is 588, so 616 fits.
So for the area of a circle: pi times radius times radius. No 2 in it, and the answer is in square units.

spec.note: Circumference = 440 m

beats.say: The circumference of a circle is 440 metres. Find its radius. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The circumference is 22 over 7 times the diameter. Think of it in parts: if the diameter is 7 parts, the circumference is 22 of the same parts.

ask.ifNot: 22 equal parts make 440. To find one part, share 440 into 22.

beats.say: The circumference, 440, is 22 parts. So how big is one part?
440 divided by 22 is 20. One part is 20 metres.
The diameter is 7 parts. 7 times 20 is 140 metres.
Stop! Is 140 our answer? The question asks for the radius, and 140 is the diameter.
The radius is half the diameter. Half of 140 is 70.
The radius is 70 metres.
Check: the diameter is 140. 140 divided by 7 is 20, and 22 times 20 is 440. It fits.

spec.note: Circumference = 176 m

beats.say: The circumference of a round park is 176 metres. Find its diameter. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The circumference is 22 over 7 times the diameter. In parts: when the diameter is 7 parts, the circumference is 22 parts.
So 22 parts make 176. One part is 176 divided by 22. 22 times 8 is 176, so one part is 8.

ask.ifNot: The diameter is 7 of those parts. So we need 7 lots of 8.

beats.say: One part is 8 metres. How do we get the diameter?
7 times 8 is 56.
The diameter of the park is 56 metres.
This time the question wants the diameter, so we stop here. Halving would give the radius, which nobody asked for.
Check: 56 divided by 7 is 8, and 22 times 8 is 176. It fits.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Find the area of a circle with radius 7 centimetres. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The area is the space inside the circle. The rule is pi times the radius times the radius.

ask.ifNot: The rule with the 2 is for the distance round. For the space inside, the radius is used twice.

beats.say: Which sum is that for our circle?
22 over 7, times 7, times 7. The radius goes in twice, and there is no 2.
One of the 7s cancels the 7 underneath. That leaves 22 times 7.
22 times 7: 20 times 7 is 140, and 2 times 7 is 14. Together, 154.
The area is 154 square centimetres.
Remember: radius times radius for area, and the answer is in square units. 154 for a radius of 7 is a number worth knowing.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Find the area of a circle with diameter 14 centimetres. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The area rule is pi times the radius times the radius. But look at what we are given.

ask.ifNot: The radius is half of the diameter. Half of 14 is what we need.

beats.say: We have the diameter, and the rule needs the radius. What is the radius?
Half of 14 is 7. That's the trap here: using 14 in the rule would make the area far too big.
Now 22 over 7, times 7, times 7. One 7 cancels the 7 underneath, leaving 22 times 7.
22 times 7: 20 times 7 is 140, and 2 times 7 is 14. Together, 154.
The area is 154 square centimetres.
Before using any circle rule, check: have I got the radius or the diameter? Then change it if you need to.

board.text: Track: radius 35 m. Distance in 3 laps = ? (π = 22/7)

spec.note: One lap is once round the track. 3 laps = ?

beats.say: A circular track has a radius of 35 metres. How far does a runner go in 3 laps? Use 22 over 7 for pi.

ask.ifNot: The runner goes round the edge of the circle. The distance round the edge is the circumference.

beats.say: One lap is once round the track. Which measure of a circle is that?
One lap is the circumference: pi times the diameter. The diameter is double the radius: 2 times 35 is 70.
Now 22 over 7, times 70. Let the 7 divide first: 70 divided by 7 is 10.
22 times 10 is 220. So one lap is 220 metres.
Don't stop at one lap! The runner goes round 3 times. 3 times 220 is 660.
The runner goes 660 metres.
Always read to the end of the question. First one lap, then as many laps as it asks for.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: This circle has a radius of 7 centimetres. Our job is to find its area. For pi we use 22 over 7.
The area is the space inside the circle. The rule is pi times the radius times the radius.

ask.ifNot: The 2 belongs to the circumference, the distance round. For the space inside, the radius is used twice: pi times 7 times 7.

beats.say: Which sum is that for our circle?
Careful: the radius goes in twice, and there is no 2 in this rule. Now let the 7 divide first. 7 divided by 7 is 1.
So we have 22 times 1 times 7. 22 times 1 is just 22.
Now 22 times 7. Split 22 into 20 and 2.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 20 times 7 is 140. 2 times 7 is 14. What do the two parts make together?
140 plus 14 makes 154.
So the area is 154 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area measures the space inside.
Does that look sensible? 7 times 7 is 49. A circle's area is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 49 is 147, so 154 fits.
So for the area of a circle: pi times radius times radius. No 2 in it, and the answer is in square units.

board.text: A diameter cuts a circle into 2 equal parts.

spec.note: The diameter cuts the circle into two equal parts

beats.say: A diameter divides a circle into two equal parts. What is each part called?

spec.note: A diameter passes through the centre

beats.say: A diameter passes straight through the centre. So the piece on one side is exactly the same as the piece on the other.

ask.ifNot: When something is shared into 2 equal parts, each part is one half.

beats.say: Two equal parts. So what fraction of the circle is each part?

board.text: each part = half of the circle

spec.note: Each part is exactly half of the circle

beats.say: Each part is half of the circle.
There is a little word that means half: semi. You may know it from semi final, the match halfway to the final.

spec.note: Half of a circle is a semicircle

beats.say: So half of a circle is called a semicircle.
An arc is only a piece of the curved edge, and a quarter circle is one of four parts. Half a circle is a semicircle.

board.text: Wheel: diameter 28 cm. Turns to cover 440 cm = ?

spec.note: How many full turns to cover 440 cm?

beats.say: A wheel has a diameter of 28 centimetres. How many complete turns will it make to cover 440 centimetres? Use 22 over 7 for pi.

ask.ifNot: In one turn the whole rim is laid out along the ground. The length of the rim is the circumference.

beats.say: Picture the wheel rolling. In one full turn, every bit of its rim touches the ground once. So how far does it move in one turn?
One turn moves the wheel forward by one circumference. That is pi times the diameter: 22 over 7, times 28.
Let the 7 divide first: 28 divided by 7 is 4. Then 22 times 4 is 88.
So each turn covers 88 centimetres. Careful: 88 is not the answer. It is the distance for one turn.
How many 88s fit into 440? 88 times 5 is 440.
The wheel makes 5 complete turns.
For rolling wheels: one turn is one circumference. Then divide the whole distance by that.

board.text: Same centre, different radii. These circles are called: ?

beats.say: Circles that have the same centre but different radii have a special name. What is it?
Different radii means different sizes: a small circle, a bigger one, a bigger one still.

choices: No, those mean the same size
ask.ifNot: Equal and congruent both mean exactly the same size. These circles have different radii, so they are different sizes.

beats.say: So could they be called equal circles, or congruent circles?
No. Those names are for circles of the same size. What is special here is that they all share one centre.
Think of a target board, or the ripples when a stone drops into a pond. Rings inside rings, all round one middle point.
Circles like that are called concentric circles. Con means together, and centric is about the centre.
So: same centre, different sizes, concentric. Listen for the word centre hiding inside the name.

spec.note: Area = 616 cm²

beats.say: The area of a circle is 616 square centimetres. Find its radius. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The area is 22 over 7, times the radius, times the radius. We know the area, so we work backwards.
To undo 22 over 7, we divide by 22 and then multiply by 7. First, 616 divided by 22 is 28.
Then 28 times 7 is 196. So radius times radius is 196.

ask.ifNot: Halving 196 will not do it. We need a number times itself. 10 times 10 is 100 and 20 times 20 is 400, so it lies between 10 and 20.

beats.say: Careful: 196 is not the radius. It is the radius times itself. Which number times itself makes 196?
It is between 10 and 20. Try 14: 14 times 10 is 140, and 14 times 4 is 56. Together, 196. Yes!
The radius is 14 centimetres.
Working backwards from an area: undo the pi, then find the number that multiplies by itself. Two steps, not one.

board.text: Circle: radius 7 cm. Which number is larger:

spec.note: Which number is larger: circumference or area?

beats.say: A circle has a radius of 7 centimetres. Looking just at the numbers, which is larger: its circumference or its area?
We can't guess, so we work out both. Circumference first: 2 times 22 over 7 times 7.
The 7s cancel, leaving 2 times 22. The circumference is 44.

ask.ifNot: Area is pi times the radius times the radius. The radius goes in twice, and there is no 2.

beats.say: Now the area. Which sum do we need?
22 over 7, times 7, times 7. One 7 cancels, leaving 22 times 7, which is 154.
Compare the two numbers. 154 is greater than 44.
So the area is the larger number: 154 is greater than 44.
One is in centimetres and the other in square centimetres, so we only compare the numbers, just as the question says.

board.text: How many radii and diameters can a circle have?

spec.note: A radius can go to any point on the circle

beats.say: How many radii and how many diameters can a circle have?

ask.ifNot: Pick any point on the circle and join it to the centre. That is a radius too. Every point gives one.

beats.say: A radius joins the centre to a point on the circle. We usually draw just one. But could we draw another, to a different point?
Yes! Every point on the circle gives a radius. And between any two points there are always more points. There is no end to them.

spec.note: A diameter can point in any direction

beats.say: Now diameters. A diameter is a straight line through the centre. Turn it a tiny bit, and you have a new diameter.
You can keep turning it by smaller and smaller amounts, for ever. So there is no end to the diameters either.
The word for no end is infinite. A circle has infinite radii and infinite diameters.
We draw one radius or one diameter to keep pictures tidy. But the circle really has endlessly many of each.

spec.note: Cut along the diameter. Perimeter of one half = ?

beats.say: Find the perimeter of a semicircle with diameter 14 centimetres. Use 22 over 7 for pi.

choices: a curved edge and a straight edge
ask.ifNot: Half a roti has a round side and a flat side where it was cut. The perimeter goes along both.

beats.say: A semicircle is half a circle, like half a roti. Walk all the way round its edge. What kinds of edge do you walk along?
A curved edge and a straight edge. That's the trap in this question: people forget the straight edge.

spec.note: Whole circle: 22/7 × 14 = 44 cm

beats.say: The curved edge is half of the whole circle's circumference. The whole circle: 22 over 7 times 14. 14 divided by 7 is 2, and 22 times 2 is 44.

spec.note: Curved edge of the half: 44 ÷ 2 = 22 cm

beats.say: Half of 44 is 22. So the curved edge is 22 centimetres.

spec.note: Straight edge: the diameter, 14 cm

beats.say: The straight edge is the diameter itself: 14 centimetres.
Add the two edges. 22 plus 14 is 36.
The perimeter of the semicircle is 36 centimetres.
Perimeter means all the way round. For a semicircle that is the curve and the flat side together.
